title: Full Workshop: Setting Yourself Up for Success —Jason Liu, OpenAI Codex

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
primary.rationale: The workshop's central focus is on designing and operating multi-agent systems within Codex: pinned threads as teammates, sub-agents, the monitor thread pattern that creates sub-threads for triage, thread-to-thread communication via list/send message tools, heartbeat automations, and the delegate skill. These are fundamentally agent loop, multi-agent, and harness architecture patterns. The three-act framework (context in, work in Codex, actions out) is an agent control-plane design. The inclusion criteria for agent_architecture_harnesses states 'Primary focus is agent loops, planning, multi-agent design, or harness architecture' and 'The talk is about the agent system, not a single tool or a single workflow engine' - this matches precisely.

secondary.label: Orchestration & Durable Execution
secondary.rationale: Heartbeat automations with configurable frequency and stopping criteria, the /goal command with verification steps, the ultra goal skill with editable goal.md and state.md work logs, and the loop skill maintaining PRs over multiple days are all durable execution patterns for long-running agent work. The Amazon refund automation running autonomously while Jason showered exemplifies crash-safe, long-running orchestration with self-regulating sleep cycles.

secondary.label: Context Engineering & Memory
secondary.rationale: The memory vault, compaction enabling 5-week-old threads with 400 sub-agents, per-project agents.md files mitigating memory bleeding, git diff for reviewing model changes to memory, and the check notes skill becoming unnecessary as the memory system matured are all context engineering and memory management patterns. The workshop devotes significant attention to how context enters the model and how state persists across long-running threads.

secondary.label: Tools, Protocols & Integrations
secondary.rationale: Skills (file-and-script constructs), plugins (libraries of skills), the Chrome extension, computer use, appshots capturing accessibility tree data, and connector integrations (Slack, Gmail, Teams, Notion, Linear) are tool-calling and integration protocol patterns. These are discussed extensively but primarily in service of the agent architecture rather than as the standalone subject.

domains.label: Personal Productivity
domains.rationale: The entire workshop is about an individual (Jason) using Codex as a personal assistant for daily productivity: managing emails, Slack, flight check-ins, form filling, video editing, code reviews, and personal CRM. The onboarding analogy and developing taste discussion reinforce the personal productivity framing.

domains.label: Developer Platforms
domains.rationale: Codex is a developer tool, and the workshop teaches developers how to set up skills, plugins, monorepo templates, and automation workflows. The personal monorepo template on GitHub and the skills ecosystem are developer-platform artifacts.

domains.label: Enterprise Operations
domains.rationale: The chief of staff automation, team-wide plugin sharing after two months of use, weekly shipping PowerPoints posted to Slack, DX triage routing, and support triage patterns touch on enterprise operations workflows, though these are primarily personal-scale implementations.

summary: Jason Liu, Developer Experience Engineer at OpenAI, presents an expanded workshop on using Codex as a general-purpose computer control tool, organized into three acts: bringing context in, working within Codex, and taking actions in the real world. For context (Act One), he details the memory vault, a personal monorepo template with agents.md redirecting code to /dev, a skills ecosystem with a skills creator and self-editing skills, plugins for Slack/Gmail/Teams/Notion/Linear, and the Chrome extension with computer use. Appshots — his favorite feature — capture the entire accessibility tree for single-function-call actions. He demonstrates voice dictation via foot pedal (roughly 3x faster than typing) and compaction enabling threads to persist five weeks with 400 sub-agents. In Act Two, pinned threads act as teammates: a chief of staff thread checks all connectors at 8am, a loop skill maintains PRs over days, and heartbeat automations with configurable frequency and stopping criteria handle support triage and other recurring tasks. The /goal command with verification steps and an ultra goal skill using editable goal.md and state.md enable adaptive long-running tasks. The monitor thread pattern extends this: a single thread identifies issues, creates sub-threads for triage, and threads can wake each other up via built-in list thread and send message tools. In Act Three, he covers writing context and taking actions: drafting emails, building slide decks, and leveraging the artifacts ecosystem (Excel, Word, PDFs, slides). In Q&A, he addresses memory bleeding (mitigated via per-project agents.md files), the onboarding analogy (expect 2-3 months before self-sufficiency), developing taste through consumption, reasoning levels (preferring low/medium over X-high maximalism), and heartbeat customization with stopping criteria — exemplified by an Amazon refund automation that recovered $400 autonomously while he showered.
whyItMatters: The software engineering and AI concepts in this workshop are facets of a single paradigm: the agent-operated development environment. The monorepo vault pattern and AGENTS.md standard provide the filesystem substrate that the memory vault, compaction, and context engineering build upon. Skills and plugins serve as the composable interface between developer workflows (PR management, code review, code migration) and AI capabilities (heartbeat automations, monitor threads, computer use). The three-act model — context in, work in Codex, actions out — shows how these concepts form a complete pipeline: context engineering (memory vault, per-project configs, git diff review) feeds into agent orchestration (pinned threads, /goal loops, monitor pattern) which drives real-world actions (appshots, computer use, thread-to-thread communication). The workshop demonstrates that the boundary between developer tooling and AI agent platform has dissolved: the same filesystem, skills, and plugins serve both purposes, and the same reasoning-level tradeoffs apply whether you are writing code or automating customer support.
temporalContext: This workshop was published on July 24, 2026, approximately five months after the Codex desktop app's February 2026 release and three months after the April 16, 2026 major update that introduced background computer use, 90+ plugins, in-app browser, memory preview, and thread automations. Jason Liu joined OpenAI in February 2026, making this workshop a product of approximately five months of intensive personal use. The personal-monorepo-template was released June 15, 2026, about five weeks before the workshop. The patterns described (chief of staff automations, heartbeat loops, monitor threads) represent community-developed workflows on top of official Codex platform capabilities as of mid-2026. Research was conducted on August 22, 2026.
takeaways: Compaction works so well that threads can run five weeks with 400 sub-agents and still retain context, overturning old advice to restart threads frequently
Appshots capture the entire accessibility tree - not just a screenshot - enabling single-function-call actions; Jason hasn't filled out a form in two weeks
Pinned threads act as teammates with automations: a chief of staff thread checks connectors at 8am, a loop skill maintains PRs over days, support triage routes issues via appshots
The monitor thread pattern enables a single thread to identify issues, create sub-threads for triage, and have threads wake each other up - extending beyond heartbeats and manual triggers
Thread-to-thread communication is available via list thread and send message tools - just ask via voice; threads can find, rename, pin, and update each other's models
X-high reasoning is overused; low and medium thinking on current models are still far superior to prior models and sufficient for most tasks including the chief of staff automation
Onboarding AI is like onboarding an employee: expect poor results on day one, invest 2-3 months of instruction and correction before it becomes self-sufficient
Develop taste by consuming more apps and experiences - you cannot describe or critique what you don't understand, just as you need to eat to develop culinary vocabulary
The chief of staff thread at 9am is the single most valuable automation to start with; a 'never stop' goal with self-regulated sleep also works well
Heartbeat automations are just text files you can edit - customize frequency by weekday/weekend, set stopping criteria, and tell threads to reply with one word when there are no updates

concepts.name: Compaction for Long-Lived Multi-Agent Threads
concepts.explanation: Context compression in Codex enables threads to persist five weeks with 400 sub-agents while retaining functional context, overturning old advice to restart threads after 20 messages.
concepts.importance: Fundamentally changes agent design assumptions; long-lived, stateful multi-agent threads become practical, enabling complex workflows that span weeks rather than single sessions.

concepts.name: Pinned Threads as Autonomous Teammates
concepts.explanation: Threads assigned persistent roles (chief of staff, agency SDK, support triage) with automations that run on schedules. Pinned threads can list, rename, pin, and message each other, functioning as team members.
concepts.importance: Represents a paradigm shift from single-conversation agents to a persistent multi-agent workforce; the chief of staff at 8am is identified as the single most valuable automation to start with.

concepts.name: Appshots and Accessibility Tree Capture
concepts.explanation: Appshots capture both an image and the entire accessibility tree (all available text including text outside the visible scroll area) from the frontmost window via macOS Accessibility permissions, enabling single-function-call actions on UI elements.
concepts.importance: Appshots are the key innovation enabling agents to interact with arbitrary GUI applications without custom integrations; Jason hasn't filled out a form in two weeks as a result.

concepts.name: Heartbeat Automations with Stopping Criteria
concepts.explanation: Scheduled recurring checks with configurable frequency (weekday vs weekend) and stopping criteria. An Amazon refund automation monitored queue wait times, adjusted checking frequency from 5-minute to 1-minute intervals, and recovered $400 autonomously while Jason showered.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates that agents can complete real-world tasks autonomously over extended periods with self-regulating behavior, bridging the gap between conversational AI and autonomous task execution.

concepts.name: Monitor Thread Pattern
concepts.explanation: A single monitor thread identifies issues and creates new sub-threads for triage. Threads can wake each other up beyond heartbeats and manual triggers, enabling a self-managing multi-agent system.
concepts.importance: Extends agent architecture beyond individual automations to a systemic monitoring and response capability; represents the state of the art in autonomous multi-agent orchestration.

concepts.name: Thread-to-Thread Communication
concepts.explanation: Codex provides built-in list thread and send message tools that enable threads to find, rename, pin, and message each other. Jason triggers this via voice: asking a thread to find a past thread, rename it, and pin it for next time.
concepts.importance: Enables truly multi-agent systems where threads collaborate and manage each other rather than operating in isolation; foundational for the monitor thread and pinned teammate patterns.

concepts.name: Memory Vault and Context Maturation
concepts.explanation: A personal memory system that accumulates context over time, learning about the user like a seven-year employee. A 'check notes' skill was used 150,000 times early on but became unnecessary after 2-3 months as the memory system took over the heavy lifting.
concepts.importance: Shows that agent memory systems improve through accumulated context and instruction, analogous to employee onboarding; early investment in memory pays compounding returns.

concepts.name: Reasoning Level Selection
concepts.explanation: Jason pushes back against X-high reasoning maximalism, advocating for low and medium thinking levels which are sufficient for most tasks including the chief of staff automation. Current models at low/medium are far superior to prior models at higher settings.
concepts.importance: Practical guidance for cost-effective agent deployment; X-high reasoning runs much longer without proportionally better results, making it a common over-optimization.

concepts.name: Computer Use for GUI Automation
concepts.explanation: Codex controls macOS/Windows applications through Screen Recording and Accessibility permissions, performing real-world actions like DocuSigning documents, faxing medical records, and filling out forms. Auto review mode is recommended for safe operation.
concepts.importance: Enables agents to interact with arbitrary applications without APIs or integrations, dramatically expanding the scope of automatable tasks; Jason prefers the desktop app specifically because everything is an appshot.

concepts.name: Goal-Directed Agent Loops with Verification
concepts.explanation: The /goal command defines verification steps that keep loops running until criteria are met. The ultra goal skill uses an editable goal.md file (editable mid-run) and a state.md work log for adaptive long-running tasks.
concepts.importance: Provides a structured way to define success criteria for autonomous agent work, enabling self-regulating loops that can adapt to changing requirements without human intervention.

concepts.name: Personal Monorepo Vault Pattern
concepts.explanation: A structured filesystem-as-database approach using projects/, people/, and .codex/skills/ directories managed from a single Codex sidebar project. The template (github.com/jxnl/personal-monorepo-template) enables managing 16+ repos from one location with per-project AGENTS.md files and git-based version control of all agent state.
concepts.importance: Provides the foundational project structure that all other patterns (memory vault, skills, pinned threads) are built upon; the filesystem IS the database for agent context, making every memory update a reviewable git commit.

concepts.name: AGENTS.md Per-Project Configuration Standard
concepts.explanation: A cross-tool standard for agent configuration files (co-developed by OpenAI Codex, Cursor, Amp, Jules, Factory) using nested files with nearest-file precedence. Jason uses per-project agents.md files to mitigate memory bleeding, e.g., specifying npm vs yarn per project.
concepts.importance: Solves the practical problem of context contamination across projects and establishes a portable, cross-tool standard for agent configuration that works across multiple AI coding tools.

concepts.name: Git Diff as Memory Audit Mechanism
concepts.explanation: Using git diff to review and audit model changes to the memory vault over time. Since the filesystem is the database, every memory update is a git commit, providing a full audit trail of what the model has learned and modified.
concepts.importance: Transforms agent memory management from a black box into a reviewable, version-controlled process; enables catching unintended modifications and security concerns in agent-maintained files.

concepts.name: Loop Skill for Long-Running PR Management
concepts.explanation: A Codex skill that maintains PRs over multiple days (e.g., Monday through Thursday), integrating reviewer feedback, rebasing, and keeping CI passing. The loop skill exemplifies durable execution patterns for agent-managed development workflows.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates that agents can manage multi-day software engineering tasks autonomously, bridging the gap between one-shot code generation and sustained engineering work with real CI constraints.

concepts.name: Skills as Composable File-and-Script Constructs
concepts.explanation: Codex skills are file-and-script constructs bundling instructions, resources, and scripts. They can self-edit, be created via a skills creator that interviews you, and be shared as team plugins after ~2 months of maturation. A 'check notes' skill was used 150,000 times early on before the memory system made it unnecessary.
concepts.importance: Skills are the primary abstraction for reusable agent workflows; their composability and self-improvement capability make them the building blocks of the entire Codex ecosystem.

concepts.name: Agent-Assisted Code Migration
concepts.explanation: Using Codex with the /goal command to migrate a rich terminal library from Python to Rust, achieving 100% test coverage on the rewritten code including UV and TypeScript components. Jason cautions this should only be done for personal experimentation, not production code at work.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates that agents can handle substantial code migration tasks with verifiable quality metrics, while also illustrating the importance of human judgment about when to apply such capabilities.

sections.title: Workshop Introduction and Goals
sections.summary: Jason introduces the workshop as an expanded, interactive version of his keynote. He covers his background at OpenAI and his use of Codex for prototyping, evals, video editing, partnerships, and operations. He emphasizes the goal of avoiding wasted tokens by sharing proven workflows and invites attendees to download Codex and clone his prepared monorepo.

sections.title: Key Takeaways: Compaction, Dictation, Memory, Skills, Pinned Threads
sections.summary: Jason presents five core takeaways: compaction works extremely well (5-week-old threads with 400 sub-agents), voice dictation via foot pedal is 3x faster than typing, appshots is his favorite feature, investing in personal memory and team plugins makes you a superhero, and pinned threads with automations act as teammates that can communicate with and manage each other.

sections.title: Three Acts of Working with AI and Audience Engagement
sections.summary: Jason frames three acts of AI work: bringing context in, working on it in Codex, and taking actions in the real world. He polls the audience on dictation usage and encourages shameless adoption, noting that messy voice memos are ideal for AI since it can cross-reference meeting notes and messages to reconstruct context.

sections.title: Skills, Plugins, and Computer Use Setup
sections.summary: Jason explains skills as simple file-and-script constructs, plugins as libraries of skills, and recommends installing plugins from the sidebar (Slack, Gmail, Teams). He strongly advocates setting up the Chrome extension and computer use, sharing his experience of Codex teaching him iMovie and placing sound effects at correct timestamps, describing it as the first time he felt AGI at work.

sections.title: Memory Vault, Appshots Deep Dive, and Skills Ecosystem
sections.summary: Jason elaborates on how the Chrome extension controls browser tabs in the background without taking over the screen. By tagging plugins and building memory over time, the AI learns about you like a seven-year employee. He details appshots capturing the entire accessibility tree for single-function-call actions. He introduces his personal monorepo template on GitHub with agents.md redirecting code to /dev. Skills can be discovered via the skill installer skill or skillset.sh, and a skills creator skill interviews you to bootstrap new ones. Standout skills include 'write like me,' DX triage, a personal CRM, and code review mimicking a colleague. He gives attendees 10 minutes to set up and takes Q&A.

sections.title: Q&A: Skill Building, Appshots, Permissions, and Security
sections.summary: Jason fields extensive Q&A. He describes using git diff to review model updates to the memory vault over days, and how AI drafts Slack responses from memory and asks permission to send. He explains his yolo one-shot approach for personal skills (built fast, self-improving) versus careful team skills shared after ~two months of use. He prefers the desktop app because everything is an appshot - summarizing videos, DocuSigning, and faxing medical records - things the CLI cannot do. He describes his job as being the AI's assistant, talking to people for context while automations run. On model choice, he uses Spark for simple computer-use tasks like flight check-in. He covers locked use (computer use with closed monitor via phone), permission modes (recommending auto review), org admin settings (blocking external emails/Slack), and security/privacy concerns. He demonstrates the delegate skill by asking another thread (Charlie) to help answer a question. He transitions to Act Two: pinned threads as teammates with heartbeat automations and the loop skill for maintaining PRs over days.

sections.title: Heartbeat Automations, /Goal, Ultra Goal, and Remote Control
sections.summary: Jason continues Act Two with live examples. Support triage uses computer use to open Twitter for escalation and checks hourly for responses. A chief of staff thread checks all connectors at 8am, surfaces the most important items with deep links, and handles flight check-ins. He describes a weekly PowerPoint of shipping items posted to Slack for the team. He recounts the iMovie bike-ride demo - Codex finds the project, reads Slack feedback, exports, uploads to Google Drive, and re-exports on new feedback. He introduces the /goal command with verification steps and the ultra goal skill using a goal.md file editable mid-run, plus a state.md work log. A Python-to-Rust migration achieved 100% test coverage. He recommends remote control via iOS app with QR code pairing. The chief of staff opens Chrome tabs for every email needing a reply during meetings. In Q&A, Jason advises letting the model write its own prompts from 10-minute voice memos, notes that project files with Slack channel IDs enable auto-discovery, addresses comparisons to OpenClaw/Hermes agents, and explains folder organization is primarily for human benefit.

sections.title: Act Three: Writing Context, Artifacts, Computer Use, and Monitor Threads
sections.summary: Jason covers Act Three - writing context and taking actions. He recommends turning on memories in settings and trying the system for a couple weeks. He highlights drafting and sending emails and Slack updates, building one-pagers and slide decks within Codex. The artifacts ecosystem renders Excel, Word docs, PDFs, and slides with annotation; his talk slides are served on the in-app browser and edited live during the presentation. He advocates using the in-app browser as the primary browser and computer use for everything else, sharing audience stories of home lab management. He warns that determined models can bypass connector limitations - using computer use to upload files when the Slack connector can't - and stresses auto review mode and agents.md guardrails. He introduces the monitor thread pattern: a single monitor thread identifies issues, creates sub-threads for triage, and threads can wake each other up beyond heartbeats and manual triggers. The sidebar serves as a hub for ongoing work streams. He details his monorepo structure: projects directory (named per workstream), people directory (every person who DM'd him), loose notes, agent summaries, and an agent-maintained to-do list. He notes the chief of staff thread at 9am is the most valuable starting point, while the to-do list automation is token-expensive and not recommended for most users.

sections.title: Final Q&A: Memory Bleeding, Onboarding, Taste, Thread Control, Reasoning Levels
sections.summary: Jason addresses final audience questions. On memory bleeding across projects, he mitigates via per-project agents.md files with specific tooling instructions (e.g., npm vs yarn). He describes a 'check notes' skill used 150,000 times early on but unneeded after 2-3 months as the memory system matured - comparing AI onboarding to employee onboarding, expecting poor initial results and gradual improvement through failure and correction. On developing taste, he advises consuming more apps and experiences to build vocabulary for critique, like eating to develop a palate. On thread-to-thread communication, he explains Codex has list thread and send message tools; via voice he asks threads to find, rename, and pin other threads, and split his slides into three act-based threads. On updating old threads to new models, he simply asks a thread to update others by model ID. On reasoning levels, he pushes back against X-high maximalism - low and medium thinking are sufficient for most tasks including the chief of staff. On silencing verbose threads, he suggests 'if no updates, reply with one word' and adjusting heartbeat frequency with stopping criteria, exemplified by an Amazon refund automation that monitored queue wait times and recovered $400 while he showered. He also describes a chief of staff variant with a 'never stop' goal that self-regulates sleep based on Jason's Slack activity.

organization.name: OpenAI
organization.summary: OpenAI is an AI research and deployment company founded in 2015. Its structure consists of the nonprofit OpenAI Foundation and the for-profit OpenAI Group PBC (public benefit corporation). OpenAI develops and maintains Codex, the AI coding agent platform that is the subject of the entire workshop. Codex is listed as a product on OpenAI's official website under the Products section alongside ChatGPT. OpenAI employs Jason Liu as a Developer Experience Engineer focused on Codex since February 2026. The company's mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity.

sources.title: Codex in ChatGPT | AI Coding Agents for Software Engineering

technologies.label: Codex Agent Platform
technologies.summary: Codex is OpenAI's AI coding agent platform available across desktop app, web, CLI, and IDE extensions. The workshop demonstrates its use as a general-purpose computer control tool organized into three acts: bringing context in, working within Codex, and taking actions in the real world. Key capabilities include appshots (accessibility tree capture for single-function-call actions), computer use (GUI automation via Screen Recording and Accessibility permissions), skills (composable file-and-script constructs), plugins (bundled skills/connectors/MCP servers with 90+ available), memory (persistent context system), compaction (long-lived threads with 400+ sub-agents persisting five weeks), in-app browser, and thread automations that resume across days or weeks.
technologies.role: Codex is the primary platform featured throughout the entire workshop. All demonstrations, patterns, and techniques are built on top of Codex capabilities. The three-act framework (context in, work in Codex, actions out) is a direct articulation of the Codex platform's control plane.

technologies.label: AGENTS.md Configuration Standard
technologies.summary: AGENTS.md is a cross-tool standard for agent configuration files co-developed by OpenAI Codex, Cursor, Amp, Jules (Google), and Factory. It supports nested files for subprojects with nearest-file precedence, enabling per-project agent configuration to prevent memory bleeding across projects. Jason Liu uses per-project agents.md files to specify tooling instructions (e.g., npm vs yarn) and isolate context across the 16+ repos managed from his personal monorepo.
technologies.role: AGENTS.md is the configuration standard Jason Liu uses for per-project agent configuration to mitigate memory bleeding across projects. It is part of the foundational setup for the personal monorepo vault pattern and is discussed during both the setup section and the final Q&A on memory management.

technologies.label: Personal Monorepo Vault Pattern
technologies.summary: A filesystem-as-database architecture where a single Codex sidebar project manages multiple repos, personal context, skills, and agent state. The personal monorepo template provides a structured layout with projects/, people/, and .codex/skills/ directories, enabling management of 16+ repos from one location with per-project AGENTS.md files and git-based version control of all agent state. Skills are composable file-and-script constructs that can self-edit, be bootstrapped via a skills creator that interviews the user, and be shared as team plugins after approximately two months of maturation.
technologies.role: The personal monorepo vault is the foundational project structure that all other patterns (memory vault, skills, pinned threads) are built upon. Jason directs attendees to clone it during the workshop setup and structures his entire Codex workflow around it.

technologies.label: Multi-Agent Thread Orchestration
technologies.summary: An agent orchestration architecture where pinned Codex threads are assigned persistent roles as teammates (chief of staff, support triage, agency SDK) with automations that run on schedules. The pattern extends to heartbeat automations with configurable frequency and stopping criteria, the /goal command with verification steps, the ultra goal skill with editable goal.md and state.md work logs, and the monitor thread pattern where a single thread identifies issues and creates sub-threads for triage. Threads can wake each other up and communicate via built-in list thread and send message tools. The chief of staff thread at 8am is identified as the single most valuable automation to start with.
technologies.role: Multi-agent thread orchestration is the central architecture pattern of Act Two of the workshop, demonstrating how pinned threads act as teammates with automations, heartbeat loops, goal-directed loops, and inter-thread communication. The chief of staff at 8am is identified as the highest-value starting point.
